md_description: This DAG represents the generation and processing of EEG data from human participants exposed to visual stimuli. It covers participant preparation, stimulus presentation timing capture, EEG acquisition, response recording, preprocessing, ERP derivation, and construction of a metadata table linking stimulus details, timing, and behavioral responses for downstream analysis of visual perception and cognition.

human_participant.reasoning: The human_participant node is an Entity, so I included only intrinsic participant-level descriptors: identity/ID, demographic, and origin/body-status fields that describe who the subject is, not what was done to them. I excluded EEG setup, stimulus, recording, preprocessing, response, and file/table properties because those belong to downstream Process, Capture, Signal, or Derivative nodes. I also avoided sample/experiment identifiers if they would overlap with downstream metadata and kept fields specific to participant provenance and biological context. No already_generated fields were provided, so there were no explicit duplication constraints beyond the node-type boundaries.

md_schema.descr: Unique human participant identifier for this recruited subject; use a stable study ID such as P001 or SUBJ_012. Assigned at enrollment and reused across all downstream EEG, stimulus, and response records for linkage.
Participant sex recorded at enrollment from self-report or study records; use for biological context in EEG/ERP analysis. Typical values: male, female, intersex, unknown.
Self-reported gender identity of the participant, if collected in the study metadata. Record at recruitment or screening. Typical values may include woman, man, nonbinary, self_described, unknown.
Participant age in years at the time of EEG session, recorded at enrollment or study visit. Use integer years; typical adult human-subject range is 18-100 in this study context.
Participant handedness recorded during screening because it may relate to neural lateralization in ERP analyses. Typical values: right, left, ambidextrous, unknown.

Vision status of the participant relevant to visual stimulus perception, recorded at screening. Typical values: normal, corrected_to_normal, impaired, unknown. Use to indicate whether glasses or contacts were used during the session.

Recruitment origin or source population for the subject, recorded at enrollment (for example university_pool, community, clinic, or online_advertisement). This describes where the participant came from, not any experimental manipulation.
Whether informed consent was obtained from the participant before EEG preparation and stimulus presentation. Record at enrollment/session start as a boolean flag.
Ordinal session index for this participant within the study, if multiple EEG visits were recorded. Use integer values such as 1, 2, 3; capture at the participant/session bookkeeping level.

High-level status indicating whether the participant reported or was screened for neurological conditions relevant to EEG interpretation. Record at screening. Typical values: none_reported, present, unknown.

eeg_cap_application.reasoning: The eeg_cap_application node is a Process, so I included only how the preparation was performed: cap/electrode setup parameters, conductive medium, reference/ground configuration, placement standard, impedance check outcome, and technician/operator details. I excluded participant intrinsic attributes because those belong to the human_participant Entity, and I excluded recording files, signals, and preprocessing outputs because those belong downstream to capture/signal nodes. I also avoided repeating any participant identifiers or general session metadata already established at the Entity layer.

md_schema.descr: EEG cap make/model used during participant preparation, recorded at the time of cap application. Use the manufacturer designation or study inventory name, for example EasyCap 64-channel. Describe the physical cap system applied to the participant.
Total number of EEG electrodes applied to the participant during cap setup, recorded immediately after fitting. Typical values in this study are 32, 64, or 128 depending on the montage.
Electrode placement convention used during cap application, recorded at setup. Typical values include 10-20, 10-10, or 10-5 system, depending on the montage used for scalp recording.
Whether conductive gel or paste was applied during electrode preparation to improve scalp contact. Record at cap application as a boolean flag.

Surface preparation performed before electrode placement, recorded during the cap application process. Typical values: none, alcohol_cleaning, abrasion, saline_sponge, other. This describes how the scalp was prepared for contact.

Reference electrode location configured during cap application, recorded as the montage reference point used for subsequent EEG acquisition. Example values include Cz, mastoid, linked_mastoids, average_reference.
Ground electrode location set during participant preparation, recorded at cap application. Use the anatomical or montage location selected for the recording setup, for example Fpz or AFz.

Maximum acceptable electrode impedance in kilo-ohms used as the quality criterion during cap application. Record the target threshold checked immediately before starting EEG recording; typical values are 5-20 kOhm.
Whether all electrodes met the impedance criterion after cap application and before stimulus presentation. Record as a boolean quality outcome for the preparation process.
Time spent fitting the cap and preparing electrodes for recording, measured from start of preparation to readiness for acquisition. Typical range is about 10-60 minutes.
Role of the person who performed the cap application, recorded during the preparation process. Typical value in this DAG is researcher or trained_technician.

prepared_participant.reasoning: The prepared_participant node is an Entity representing the participant state after EEG setup, so I included only readiness/status descriptors that summarize the prepared subject itself: whether setup is complete, whether the participant is fit to proceed, and the immediate preparation outcome. I excluded cap/electrode parameters and preparation procedure details because those belong to the eeg_cap_application Process, and I excluded stimulus, EEG acquisition, and response details because those belong to downstream Capture nodes. I also avoided repeating participant identity or demographic fields already owned by human_participant.

md_schema.descr: Overall readiness of the participant after EEG setup and before stimulus presentation, recorded immediately after cap application. Typical values: ready, delayed, not_ready, requires_adjustment.
Boolean flag indicating whether EEG setup was completed successfully and the participant was cleared to begin the visual ERP task. Record at the end of preparation before any stimulus is presented.

High-level assessment of scalp-electrode contact quality after preparation, recorded before acquisition begins. Typical values: good, acceptable, poor, unknown. This summarizes contact adequacy, not individual impedance values.
Participant comfort state after EEG setup and before task onset, captured by the operator at the end of preparation. Typical values: comfortable, mild_discomfort, discomfort, unknown.
Whether the participant was instructed and acknowledged the need to minimize movement during EEG recording and stimulus presentation. Record at the preparation endpoint as a boolean flag.
Boolean indicator that the prepared participant can proceed to visual stimulus presentation and EEG recording without further setup changes. Record immediately before the capture phase begins.

Free-text or coded note summarizing any residual preparation issues that still characterize the prepared participant state, such as minor adjustment needed or glasses placed for corrected vision. Use this only for brief status context at readiness time.

visual_stimulus_presentation.reasoning: I removed the colliding field operator_role because it was already generated for an earlier DAG step, and kept only capture-specific settings for the visual stimulus presentation session. The remaining fields describe configured display hardware, timing, geometry, software, and ambient presentation conditions, which are within the Capture node's territory and do not duplicate stimulus-log, participant, or response metadata.

md_schema.descr: Manufacturer of the display device used to present visual stimuli during the session, recorded at the time of stimulus presentation setup. Example: Dell, ASUS, ViewSonic. This describes the hardware actively configured for the capture session.
Model name or number of the display used for visual stimulus presentation, recorded during setup. Example: U2415 or VG279. Use the model identifier specified by the operator.
Display refresh rate in hertz configured for the presentation session, measured/verified before stimulus onset. Typical values are 60, 120, 144, or 240 Hz; this affects stimulus timing precision.
Horizontal pixel resolution of the display used for stimulus presentation, recorded at setup. Example: 1920 px. Use the configured screen width before the task begins.
Vertical pixel resolution of the display used for stimulus presentation, recorded at setup. Example: 1080 px. Use the configured screen height before the task begins.
Software or task engine used to present stimuli and control timing, recorded at the capture setup stage. Example: PsychoPy, Presentation, E-Prime, Psychtoolbox.
Version of the stimulus presentation software used for the session, recorded alongside the software name at setup. Example: 2024.1 or 3.0.5.
How visual stimuli were delivered to the participant during the capture session. Typical values: full_screen, windowed, mirrored_display, projector.
Approximate distance from the participant's eyes to the display during stimulus presentation, measured or set before the session. Typical range is about 30-150 cm depending on the apparatus.

Method used to control stimulus onset and duration during presentation. Typical values: screen_refresh_locked, software_timer, hardware_trigger, mixed. Record the configuration used to enforce timing.

Display luminance setting in candela per square meter used during the stimulus presentation session, measured or calibrated before task onset. Typical range is roughly 1-300 cd/m2 depending on the display and experiment.
Ambient room light condition during visual stimulus presentation, recorded as an operator-controlled capture setting. Typical values: dark, low, moderate, bright.

stimulus_timing_log.reasoning: The stimulus_timing_log node is a Signal, so I included only raw digital artefact properties: file format, file size, temporal and row-level dimensions, sampling/clock precision, storage location, integrity, and whether it is complete. I excluded stimulus hardware/configuration details because those belong to the upstream visual_stimulus_presentation Capture, and I excluded interpreted or derived trial-level summaries because those would belong downstream to a Derivative. I also avoided the previously generated operator_role field and any participant identifiers or response fields.

md_schema.descr: Digital file format of the raw stimulus timing log produced by the presentation system, recorded for the stored artefact. Examples include csv, tsv, json, or log. Capture this from the saved log file itself.
Size of the raw timing log file in bytes, measured on the stored artefact after the presentation session. Use this as a basic completeness and transfer-check metric.

Number of stimulus trials represented in the raw timing log file, counted from the stored log contents after capture. Typical values depend on the task design and may range from tens to hundreds of trials.
Total number of rows in the raw stimulus timing log file, counted in the stored digital artefact. This may differ from n_trials_logged if the log includes header rows or auxiliary events.

Clock or reference used to express onset and duration values in the log, recorded from the file metadata or log header. Typical values: seconds_since_start, milliseconds_since_start, absolute_timestamp.

Smallest practical temporal precision of the logged onset/duration timestamps in milliseconds, inferred from the digital artefact or logger output. Typical values are 1, 0.1, or 0.01 ms depending on the system.
Filesystem or object-store path where the raw stimulus timing log is saved, recorded for data management and retrieval. Example: /data/sub-001/stimulus_timing_log.csv or s3://bucket/path/file.json.
SHA-256 checksum of the raw timing log file, recorded after saving to verify file integrity and detect transfer corruption.
Whether the raw timing log contains the expected stimulus events and is considered complete enough for downstream ERP analysis. Assess on the stored file after capture, before any preprocessing.
How display conditions are encoded in the raw log file, recorded from the artefact structure. Typical values: explicit_columns, event_codes, mixed, unknown.

eeg_recording.reasoning: The eeg_recording node is a Capture, so I included only actively configured acquisition-session and amplifier/instrument settings that govern how the EEG was collected: amplifier hardware, sampling, filter settings, channel count, reference/ground configuration, and recording-mode details. I excluded participant attributes, stimulus timing, and behavioral responses because those belong to upstream Entity/Capture nodes or other measurement streams. I also excluded raw file properties and derived quality summaries because those belong to the raw_eeg_signal Signal. I did not repeat any previously generated fields, including operator_role, which was already produced for an earlier process node.

md_schema.descr: Manufacturer of the EEG amplifier used for scalp electrical recording, recorded at the time of acquisition setup. Example: Brain Products, BioSemi, g.tec. This identifies the hardware actively configured for the session.
Model name or number of the EEG amplifier used during recording, recorded during acquisition setup. Example: ActiCHamp, ActiveTwo, g.HIamp.
Serial number of the EEG amplifier used in this recording session, recorded to uniquely identify the hardware unit. Use the device serial as labeled by the manufacturer.
EEG sampling rate in hertz configured for acquisition, measured/verified at the start of recording. Typical values include 250, 500, 1000, or 2048 Hz depending on the system.
Low cutoff frequency of the online bandpass filter applied during EEG acquisition, recorded in hertz at recording setup. Typical values are 0.01-1 Hz for the low cutoff.
High cutoff frequency of the online bandpass filter applied during EEG acquisition, recorded in hertz at recording setup. Typical values are 30-100 Hz depending on the recording scheme.
Number of EEG channels actively recorded during the session, recorded at acquisition setup. Typical values are 32, 64, 128, or 256 depending on the montage.
Reference configuration used during online EEG acquisition, recorded at the start of recording. Typical values include Cz, mastoid, linked_mastoids, or average_reference.
Ground electrode configuration used during the EEG recording session, recorded at acquisition setup. Describe the grounding approach or location used by the amplifier system.
Acquisition mode used for EEG collection. Typical values: continuous, segmented, triggered, or hybrid; record the mode chosen for the session.
Whether electrode impedances were checked during acquisition, recorded as an acquisition-session quality control flag. This indicates if impedance monitoring occurred while recording.
Whether hardware triggers were enabled for time-locking EEG acquisition to stimulus events, recorded at acquisition setup. Use true if event markers were captured directly by the acquisition system.

raw_eeg_signal.reasoning: This is the raw_eeg_signal Signal node, so I kept only raw EEG artefact properties that were not already used elsewhere in the DAG. Because file_format, file_size_bytes, sampling_rate_hz, storage_path, and checksum_sha256 were already generated for earlier signal steps, I replaced them with non-colliding raw-signal fields focused on dimensions, channel structure, temporal span, and technical completeness. I excluded capture settings, preprocessing details, and any participant/stimulus interpretation because those belong upstream or downstream, not to the raw signal artefact itself.

md_schema.descr: Number of EEG channels present in the raw continuous recording file, counted from the stored artefact after acquisition. Use the channel count encoded in the file or header; typical values are 32, 64, 128, or 256.
Total number of time samples in the raw EEG signal file, counted across the continuous recording stored after acquisition. This is a raw artefact dimension, not a sampling configuration setting.

Total duration of the raw continuous EEG recording in seconds, derived from the stored artefact length. Record the full span of the file after acquisition, typically from tens of minutes to a few hours.
Numeric precision of the stored EEG samples in bits, taken from the raw file encoding or header. Typical values are 16, 24, or 32 and indicate the raw storage precision of the signal values.
Physical unit used for the raw EEG sample values in the stored file. Typical values include uV, V, or arbitrary_units, depending on the acquisition export.
Labeling convention used for the EEG channels in the raw signal file, recorded from the artefact header. Typical values include 10-20, 10-10, montage_specific, or custom.
Whether the raw EEG file is complete and spans the expected recording period without truncation or missing sections. Assess this on the stored artefact after acquisition.

High-level technical assessment of the raw EEG artefact based on the stored file only. Typical values: usable, noisy, partial, corrupted, unknown. This is not a preprocessing or scientific quality score.

Whether the raw EEG file contains embedded artifact annotations or event markers in addition to the continuous signal, recorded from the file contents. Use true if such annotations are present in the raw artefact.

response_collection.reasoning: The response_collection node is a Capture, so I included only the actively configured behavioral response setup: device type and manufacturer/model, button mapping, timing mode, and operator-controlled session settings. I excluded the raw response event file properties because those belong to the downstream response_event_signal Signal, and I excluded participant identity or stimulus metadata because those belong to other nodes. I also avoided all previously generated field names, including those already used for capture/session instrumentation elsewhere in the DAG.

md_schema.descr: Manufacturer of the response input device used to collect participant behavioral responses, recorded at setup. Example: Cedrus, Current Designs, RB-740. This identifies the hardware actively configured for response capture.
Model name or number of the response device used during the task, recorded at setup. Example: Lumina, RB series, button box model identifier.
Type of response device used to collect participant behavioral responses during the visual task. Typical values: button_box, keyboard, mouse, joystick, touchpad, touchscreen, other.
How physical buttons or keys were mapped to response options during the capture session, recorded before task onset. Example values: left_right, yes_no, 1_2, custom, or counterbalanced.
How responses were registered during the task, recorded at the response collection setup stage. Typical values: discrete_button_press, continuous_rating, multi_choice, free_keypress.
Timing strategy used to record response events relative to the stimulus task, recorded at setup. Typical values: event_driven, polling, hardware_triggered, mixed.
If responses were polled rather than event-driven, the polling rate in hertz configured for response capture. Typical values are 50-1000 Hz depending on the device and software.
Start of the allowed response window relative to stimulus onset, in milliseconds, configured for the task. Typical range can be negative for pre-stimulus baselines or positive post-onset windows.
End of the allowed response window relative to stimulus onset, in milliseconds, configured for the task. Use the task definition applicable to response capture.
Software used to present the response interface and record behavioral responses, recorded at setup. Example: PsychoPy, Presentation, E-Prime, custom Python task.
Version of the response capture software used in the session, recorded alongside the software name. Example: 2024.1 or 3.0.5.

response_event_signal.reasoning: The response_event_signal node is a Signal, so I included only raw artefact properties of the behavioral response file: file format, size, row/sample counts, temporal reference, storage location, integrity, and a basic completeness indicator. I excluded response device setup and timing configuration because those belong to the upstream response_collection Capture, and I excluded interpreted response accuracy or summary statistics because those belong to downstream derivatives or analysis tables. I also avoided all previously generated field names, including file-level identifiers already used in other Signal nodes.

md_schema.descr: Digital file format of the raw behavioral response event record saved after the task. Examples include csv, tsv, json, log, or txt. Record the on-disk format of the response artefact.
Size of the raw response event file in bytes, measured on the stored artefact after capture. Use this as a technical descriptor of the response record.
Total number of response events recorded in the raw file, counted from the stored artefact. Includes button presses or other behavioral events with timestamps.
Clock or reference used for response timestamps in the raw event file. Typical values: milliseconds_since_start, seconds_since_start, absolute_timestamp, or trial_relative.
Smallest practical temporal precision of the response timestamps in milliseconds, inferred from the raw event file or logger output. Typical values are 1, 0.1, or 0.01 ms.
Filesystem or object-store path where the raw response event file is stored. Example: /data/sub-001/response_events.csv or s3://bucket/path/file.json.
SHA-256 checksum of the raw response event file, recorded for integrity verification after storage or transfer.
Whether the raw response event file contains the expected behavioral events for the session and is considered complete for downstream analysis. Assess this on the stored artefact after capture.
Whether response events appear in a valid chronological order in the raw file, assessed from the stored artefact. Use true if timestamps are monotonic or the logger preserved event order.
Brief technical description of the raw response record structure, such as one_row_per_event, one_row_per_trial, or mixed. This describes the stored signal representation, not the behavioral meaning.

eeg_preprocessing.reasoning: The eeg_preprocessing node is a Process, so I included only transformation parameters and software configuration used to convert raw EEG into cleaned epochs: filter settings, artifact handling, epoch windowing, baseline correction, rereferencing, and software agent details. I excluded raw signal properties and file-specific descriptors because those belong to the upstream raw_eeg_signal Signal, and I excluded the cleaned epoch file properties because those belong to the downstream cleaned_eeg_epochs Signal. I also avoided repeating any field ids already generated elsewhere in the DAG, including operator-style names and storage/file identifiers.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software package used for EEG preprocessing, recorded for the transformation step. Example: EEGLAB, MNE-Python, FieldTrip, BrainVision Analyzer.
Version of the preprocessing software used to filter, clean, and epoch the EEG data, recorded at processing time. Example: 2024.0, 1.7, 2023.2.
High-pass filter cutoff in hertz applied during EEG preprocessing, recorded as the lower frequency bound of the cleaning pipeline. Typical values are 0.1-1 Hz for ERP preprocessing.
Low-pass filter cutoff in hertz applied during EEG preprocessing, recorded as the upper frequency bound of the cleaning pipeline. Typical values are 30-40 Hz for ERP preprocessing.

Mains noise notch filter frequency in hertz applied during preprocessing, if used. Typical values are 50 or 60 Hz depending on local power frequency; use 0 or null-equivalent coding only if your data model requires a numeric value.
Primary method used to detect or remove artifacts during preprocessing. Typical values: manual_rejection, thresholding, ICA, automated_mixing, combined.
Start of the epoch window relative to stimulus onset in milliseconds, defined during preprocessing for ERP analysis. Typical ERP windows include values such as -200 ms.
End of the epoch window relative to stimulus onset in milliseconds, defined during preprocessing for ERP analysis. Typical ERP windows often extend to 800 ms or 1000 ms post-onset.
Time window in milliseconds used for baseline correction during preprocessing, relative to stimulus onset. Typical values are a pre-stimulus interval such as -200 to 0 ms.
Method used to re-reference EEG during preprocessing. Typical values: average, mastoid, linked_mastoids, Cz, none.
Whether independent component analysis or similar component removal was used to remove artifacts during preprocessing. Record true if components were explicitly removed.
How noisy or invalid channels were handled during preprocessing. Typical values: interpolated, removed, retained, none.
Type of event used to create task-related epochs during preprocessing, recorded as the event lock used for segmentation. Example: stimulus_onset, response_onset, cue_onset.
Whether preprocessing completed successfully and produced task-related epochs suitable for ERP analysis. Record at the end of the preprocessing step.

cleaned_eeg_epochs.reasoning: The cleaned_eeg_epochs node is a Signal, so I kept only raw artefact descriptors for the epoched EEG output and renamed colliding fields to be node-specific. I excluded preprocessing parameters because those belong to eeg_preprocessing, and I avoided repeating previously generated generic file fields by using epoch-specific names for storage and integrity details. The schema now focuses on what the saved epoched EEG artefact contains and its basic technical completeness, without overlapping earlier Signal metadata.

md_schema.descr: Digital file format of the cleaned epoched EEG data saved after preprocessing. Examples include set, fif, mat, or h5. Record the on-disk format of the epoched signal file.
Size of the cleaned EEG epoch file in bytes, measured on the stored artefact after preprocessing. Use this as a technical descriptor of the epoched data object.
Number of EEG epochs contained in the cleaned epoched data file, counted after preprocessing and artifact handling. Typical values depend on trial count and rejection rate.
Duration of each EEG epoch in milliseconds, as stored in the cleaned epoched dataset. For fixed-length epochs this is the same across trials; typical ERP epochs are 500-1200 ms long.
Number of EEG channels retained in the cleaned epoched dataset, counted after preprocessing. This may match the original montage or be reduced after bad-channel removal.
Sampling rate in hertz represented in the cleaned epoched EEG data, preserved from the raw signal or preprocessing output. Record the effective sampling rate of the epoched file.
Filesystem or object-store path where the cleaned EEG epoch file is stored. Example: /data/sub-001/cleaned_epochs.set or s3://bucket/path/file.fif.
SHA-256 checksum of the cleaned EEG epoch file, recorded for integrity verification after storage or transfer.
Whether the cleaned epoched dataset contains the expected task epochs for the session and is considered complete for ERP analysis. Assess on the stored artefact after preprocessing.

High-level technical quality assessment of the cleaned epoched dataset, such as usable, sparse, partial, or corrupted, based on the stored artefact only. This is a raw technical quality indicator, not a scientific interpretation.

Number of trials or epochs rejected during preprocessing before saving the cleaned epoched dataset, counted from the output artefact or preprocessing summary. Use this to summarize retained data extent.
Whether baseline correction was applied to the cleaned EEG epochs during preprocessing. Record true if the epoched data were baseline adjusted before storage.

erp_computation.reasoning: The erp_computation node is a Process, so I included only the computation method and parameters used to derive ERPs from cleaned epochs and timing logs: averaging scheme, event-lock definition, baseline handling, channel/condition aggregation, and software agent details. I excluded raw EEG file properties and stimulus timing records because those belong to upstream Signal nodes, and I excluded ERP output file properties because those belong to the downstream erp_waveforms Derivative. I also avoided repeating any previously generated field names, including generic software/version and quality fields used on other nodes.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software package used to compute event-related potentials from epoched EEG. Example: MNE-Python, EEGLAB, FieldTrip, custom Python pipeline.
Version of the ERP computation software used during the averaging step, recorded at processing time. Example: 1.7, 2024.0, 3.0.5.
Event type used to time-lock epochs for ERP averaging, recorded for the computation step. Example values: stimulus_onset, response_onset, cue_onset. This defines the alignment point for the ERP.
Method used to combine epochs into ERP waveforms, recorded during computation. Typical values: simple_mean, weighted_mean, robust_mean, trimmed_mean.
Time window in milliseconds used for baseline handling during ERP computation, typically a pre-event interval such as -200 to 0 ms. Record the exact window applied before averaging.
How trials or epochs were grouped into ERP conditions during computation. Typical values: by_stimulus_category, by_response_type, by_trial_type, custom.
Number of ERP conditions generated in the computation step, counted from the grouped epochs used for averaging. Typical values depend on the task design and experimental contrasts.
Whether artifact-contaminated epochs were excluded from the ERP averaging step. Record true if rejected epochs were omitted during computation.
How channels were handled during ERP computation. Typical values: per_channel, region_of_interest, global_average, reference_channel_only.
Whether ERP computation completed successfully and produced the expected condition- and channel-level averages. Record at the end of the processing step.
Temporal alignment convention used when generating the ERP, such as zero at stimulus onset. Use this to describe how the time axis of the averages was defined during computation.

erp_waveforms.reasoning: The erp_waveforms node is a Derivative, so I kept only computed-output descriptors of the ERP artefact itself: output format, file size, output dimensions, time-axis bounds and resolution, storage location, integrity, and derivative-specific quality/label metadata. I removed any fields that collided with prior DAG steps, specifically n_conditions and n_channels, and I continued to exclude upstream computation parameters and raw signal properties because those belong to the process and signal nodes. The remaining fields describe the derived waveform file as a reusable analysis object without duplicating earlier metadata.

md_schema.descr: Digital file format of the derived ERP waveform artefact, as stored after computation. Examples include csv, tsv, mat, fif, or h5. Record the on-disk format of the ERP output.
Size of the ERP waveform output file in bytes, measured on the stored derivative artefact after computation. Use this as a technical descriptor of the derived data object.
Number of time samples or time bins in each ERP waveform, counted from the derived output file. This reflects the temporal resolution of the computed ERP traces.
Start time of the ERP waveform time axis in milliseconds relative to the locking event, as represented in the derived output. Typical values are negative for pre-event baseline periods.
End time of the ERP waveform time axis in milliseconds relative to the locking event, as represented in the derived output. Typical ERP waveforms extend several hundred milliseconds post-event.

Temporal spacing between adjacent ERP samples or time bins in milliseconds, measured from the derived waveform output. Typical values depend on the sampling rate and any resampling performed during derivation.
Filesystem or object-store URI where the derived ERP waveform artefact is stored. Example: /results/sub-001/erp_waveforms.csv or s3://bucket/path/file.mat.
SHA-256 checksum of the derived ERP waveform file, recorded for integrity verification after computation and storage.

High-level quality assessment of the derived ERP waveforms, such as usable, low_snr, partial, or corrupted, based on the computed output only. This is a derivative quality indicator, not a raw technical flag.

Labels or codes identifying the ERP conditions represented in the derived waveform output, recorded from the output artefact. Use a compact representation such as an array-encoded string or delimiter-separated list if your schema requires a scalar field.

metadata_table_building.reasoning: The metadata_table_building node is a Process, so I included only how the trial-level table was assembled: join keys, record alignment, row construction rules, and software/tooling used for the merge. I excluded the stimulus, timing, response, and ERP content itself because those belong to the upstream Signal/Derivative nodes being combined, and I excluded the final table's storage or schema properties because those belong to the downstream trial_metadata_table Derivative. I also avoided all previously generated field ids, including generic software/version, operator, file, and channel/count fields.

md_schema.descr: Name of the software package or library used to assemble the trial-level metadata table. Example: Python pandas, R dplyr, SQL pipeline, custom ETL script.
Version of the table-building software or library used during metadata assembly, recorded at processing time. Example: 2.2, 1.5.3, 2024.0.

Key fields used to align stimulus timing records, behavioral responses, and ERP-related records when building the trial metadata table. Example values may include trial_id, stimulus_id, response_id, or a composite key encoded as text.
Unit of observation represented by each row in the assembled metadata table. Typical values: trial, stimulus_event, participant_trial, condition_trial.
Method used to combine source records into the final trial-level table. Typical values: inner_join, left_join, outer_join, keyed_merge, custom_merge.
Rule applied when multiple source records map to the same trial during table construction. Typical values: first_keep, last_keep, aggregate, drop_duplicates, manual_review.
Policy used to handle missing stimulus, timing, or response fields during metadata table construction. Typical values: retain_nulls, impute_defaults, exclude_trial, flag_missing, custom.
Maximum allowable mismatch in milliseconds when aligning stimulus timing and response records into a common trial row, if time-based matching was used. Typical values are small, such as 1-50 ms.
Number of stimulus timing records consumed from the upstream log during metadata table assembly, counted before merging. Use this as a provenance count for the input stream.
Number of behavioral response records consumed from the upstream response event signal during metadata table assembly, counted before merging. Use this as a provenance count for the input stream.
Number of rows written to the assembled trial-level metadata table, counted at the end of the building process. This reflects the final table cardinality.
Whether the metadata table assembly finished successfully and produced the expected trial-level output. Record at the end of the process.

trial_metadata_table.reasoning: The trial_metadata_table node is a Derivative, so I kept only properties intrinsic to the final table artefact: output format, size, column count, storage location, key column presence, completeness, and table-level quality. I removed colliding fields n_rows and row_granularity because they were already generated elsewhere in the DAG. I also excluded upstream stimulus/response content and table-building process details because those belong to other nodes, not the final derivative table.

md_schema.descr: Digital file format of the trial-level metadata table as stored after assembly. Examples include csv, tsv, parquet, xlsx, or h5. Record the on-disk format of the derived table.
Size of the trial-level metadata table file in bytes, measured on the stored derivative artefact after assembly. Use this as a technical descriptor of the derived table.
Number of columns in the final metadata table, counted from the stored artefact. Include all stimulus, timing, response, and linking fields present in the derived table.
Whether the final metadata table contains a dedicated trial identifier column for linking across records. Record true if a unique per-trial ID is present.
Whether the final metadata table contains a stimulus identifier column linking rows to stimulus events or stimulus descriptions. Record true if present in the derived table.
Whether the final metadata table includes a response type or response category column. Record true if behavioral response type is explicitly included.
Whether the final metadata table includes a stimulus onset time column. Record true if presentation timing is represented explicitly in the derived table.
Total number of missing or null cells in the final metadata table, counted from the stored artefact. Use this as a basic completeness indicator for the derived table.

High-level quality assessment of the final metadata table, such as usable, incomplete, inconsistent, or corrupted, based on the derived artefact only. This is a table-level quality indicator, not a source-data flag.
Filesystem or object-store URI where the derived trial metadata table is stored. Example: /results/sub-001/trial_metadata_table.csv or s3://bucket/path/table.parquet.
